analysis.one_liner: Bans U.S. gasoline exports whenever domestic prices top $3.12 a gallon.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Foreign Affairs Committee with no cosponsors and no action since its April 2026 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the President to prohibit exports of gasoline made in the United States during periods when the average national price is $3.12 per gallon or higher for seven straight days. The idea is to keep more of the domestic fuel supply at home when drivers are paying high prices. The President could grant exemptions for exports he decides serve the national interest, and the prohibition would end once prices stayed below the threshold for seven days. It was introduced in April 2026 and referred to the House Foreign Affairs Committee, where no further action has been taken. [S2] [S3] [S5]
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, American drivers would benefit whenever pump prices hit the $3.12 trigger, because gasoline that would otherwise be sold to foreign buyers would stay in the domestic market, adding supply when prices are high. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: During any period when the average U.S. gasoline price has been at or above $3.12 per gallon for seven consecutive days, the President must prohibit exports of U.S.-produced gasoline, keeping that fuel in the domestic market.
The trigger ends automatically once prices have been below $3.12 for seven straight days, so the ban applies only during stretches of high prices.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners and gasoline exporters would lose the ability to sell U.S.-produced gasoline to foreign buyers during high-price periods, cutting into export revenue. Refining margins typically depend on selling into export markets when domestic demand is saturated, so the cost would fall on the refining and export business. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the President broad discretion to exempt exports he determines are consistent with the national interest, and to set terms and conditions, so the ban's strength depends entirely on how a given administration uses that authority.

The bill defines gasoline narrowly as one tariff-classification category, and U.S. gasoline prices are set in a global market, so a temporary export ban may move pump prices less than its supporters suggest while still cutting export revenue for refiners.

Cutting refiners' access to export markets during high-price periods could reduce the profitability that supports domestic refining capacity, an effect that over time could work against the supply it is meant to protect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's goal — more fuel at home when prices spike — is popular and straightforward, but its design is weak: the price trigger is automatic rather than tied to supply conditions, the President can exempt nearly any export, and because gasoline trades in a global market, the effect on pump prices is uncertain while the hit to refiners' export business is certain. An honest supporter would acknowledge this is as much a signal bill as a working price tool.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2026 and referred to the House Foreign Affairs Committee, which has taken no action on it; with no cosponsors and no scheduled hearing or vote, it is sitting in committee.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the Gasoline Export Ban Act of 2026 on April 14, 2026.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.
No cosponsors joined the bill from either party.
The committee has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, oil refiners and gasoline exporters are better off: no export ban has moved, so the ability to sell U.S. gasoline into higher-priced foreign markets during price spikes remains intact. Drivers have gained nothing yet, because the bill has not advanced.

for.name: Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Brian Mast
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for any committee hearing or markup since it was referred in April 2026.

sides.party_line_note: No one joined from either party — the bill has zero cosponsors among 217 Democrats, 1 independent, and 223 Republicans — so no partisan pattern can be read yet; the only action so far is that a Republican-run committee has not taken it up. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: The bill would bar them from selling U.S. gasoline abroad during any stretch when domestic prices sit at or above $3.12 a gallon, cutting export revenue precisely when export markets pay most. Their interest in keeping export markets open runs against drivers' interest in lower pump prices. [S2] [S3] [S4]—the bill's stillbirth leaves their export business untouched.
Drivers would see the benefit only if the bill advanced, which it has not; the extra domestic supply would apply only during high-price stretches. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action two-plus months after introduction, the bill is very likely to die quietly in committee, the way most single-sponsor foreign-trade bills do. Advancing would require the Foreign Affairs chair to schedule a markup, which nothing in the record suggests will happen.
